extracted.intended_audience: prospective society editors and newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters and society editors on preparing society-page copy, following up and rewriting news stories, and writing feature (human-interest) pieces. Covers sourcing, typographical style, follow-up and rewrite techniques, and feature-story craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clubs coverage (constructive society news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give special attention to women's clubs and their work in literature, education, community betterment, general social relief, and kindred subjects; these offer a vast undeveloped field for constructive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid filling the society page with dull routine items; feature what women are doing (e.g., study of the garbage question, campaigns against flies, comforts for unprivileged slum children) with attractive individual heads to interest intelligent readers and build a constructive department in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style for society columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow at first the typographical style of the society column in your paper; papers differ in whether each event gets a separate head or everything is grouped under 'Society' with paragraph breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing lists of names, group like names and titles together: married couples first, then married women whose names appear alone, then unmarried women, and finally the men. Be prepared for paragraphs half-column long or varied paragraphing depending on house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify announcements; avoid spurious announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept announcements of engagements, marriages, and births from anyone except the immediate persons concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of telephone announcements and practical jokes; many papers use printed forms mailed to families requiring signatures for announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for society news and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate reliable sources (social leaders, friendly acquaintances) but rely especially on caterers, florists, and hair-dressing parlors for advance notice of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visit or call these businesses regularly to stay abreast of society news. Always be absolutely sure of addresses, names, and initials — errors quickly produce trouble (e.g., angry relatives complaining to the city editor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: follow-ups vs rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Follow-ups' contain news in addition to that of the original story; 'rewrites' are only revisions of previously printed material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the distinction: follow-ups add newly developed facts; rewrites re-present old facts freshly. Most stories are incomplete on first appearance and may require follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive role of follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter must not consider a story ended until all possibilities are run to ground; the follow-up is an opportunity for constructive journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow investigations, scientific work, public-health developments, strikes, wrecks, fires, graft/crime exposures, etc., over weeks or months to provide educational and lasting value beyond sensational initial figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following up a story: first steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigned a follow-up, read the whole original story carefully and be familiar with the news so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the first reporter played up the real feature or missed a better one; familiarity with all local news is expected of reporters at all times.

rubrics_metrics.name: New facts should be featured in follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the follow-up should feature newly learned facts — e.g., funeral arrangements after a sudden death, investigation and placement of blame after a wreck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the new facts the focus of the lead and treatment of the follow-up story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature results in follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the lead of a follow-up should emphasize the results effected by the details of the earlier story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., economic or market consequences the day after a government crop report; show chain of causation from the earlier item to present effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable results when new facts are scarce
rubrics_metrics.description: When no more important details can be learned, it may be wise to feature probable results as the lead of a follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative expectation or official belief to present likely consequences (e.g., probable diplomatic break, anticipated investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clues for identification in crime follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: In crime stories where offenders have escaped, the lead to the follow-up may begin with clues to establish identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide distinctive descriptive clues (e.g., 'piano tuner about forty...silver spectacles...') to solicit public help and maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature absence of new information where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the fact that there is no additional news is itself worth featuring in a follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a lack-of-news lead when the continuing uncertainty or absence of developments is newsworthy to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opinions of prominent persons
rubrics_metrics.description: An otherwise unimportant follow-up may be strengthened by interviewing prominent persons and localizing interest in figures readers know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote authorities or local leaders to give weight or local relevance to the follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of opinions for perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview a number of local persons and present a summary of their differing views when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A summary lead of widely differing opinions (e.g., on an ethical issue) can provide useful context and represent community reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include connecting links immediately after the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sufficient explanatory matter to connect the follow-up incidents with preceding events, because many readers will have missed earlier stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place these connecting links in or immediately after the lead to give the reader necessary bearings before continuing with the new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites: make old news new and avoid resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: A rewrite should present a story of which priority has been gained by another paper in such a way that it bears no resemblance to the other paper's copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewriters must find new features, new angles, new relations among details, or fresh phrasing; they are among the most skillful reporters on a daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring a rewrite 'up to the minute'
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite in rewriting is to make old news seem current; present events so that they appear timely for the paper's readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid time words like 'yesterday' in the lead; reframe leads to place the event in relation to the paper's publication time (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek new features when rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: In rewriting, seek a new feature: bring the story up to date, look for overlooked features, anticipate probable developments, or relate the incident to similar recent events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagination but remain truthful; consider motives, causes, other agencies, or patterns that add new light to old news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation in rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrites are generally shorter than originals (often from a half to a fourth the length) and should be cut down firmly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut 'to the bone' when rewriting, but do not merely omit paragraphs — excision is not rewriting; ensure the rewrite reads as fresh, not merely shorter.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a feature story is (human-interest purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature (human-interest) story makes items of little news value interesting by appealing to emotions and employing literary craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The feature's news value is often less excellent than a lead news story; it needs a 'touch of literary rouge' — centering interest in a single emotion and diverting attention from dull details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and need for restraint in human-interest features
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-interest features are difficult because of the temptation to overemphasize; only artists can handle them successfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint is required to avoid caricature (overdone humor) or inducing derisive laughter (overdone pathos). A single misplaced word or phrase can destroy the entire effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two main types: the emotional (human-interest) type whose purpose is largely to entertain by appealing to emotions, and the instructive type whose purpose is to instruct or inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emotional type derives interest from elemental instincts (love, fear, hate, etc.); the instructive type appeals to curiosity and derives interest from the information conveyed.
